claims.text: The Salton Sea is the largest lake in California by surface area.
The modern lake was formed from an inflow of water from the Colorado River in 1905.
Beginning in 1900, an irrigation canal was dug from the Colorado River to provide water to the Imperial Valley for farming.

In 1905, heavy rainfall and snowmelt caused the Colorado River to swell, and the flood poured down the canal; over about two years, two newly created rivers carried the entire volume of the Colorado River into the Salton Sink.
On February 11, 1907, the breach was finally closed.
The lake would have dried out naturally during the early 20th century, but local farmers used generous amounts of Colorado River water for irrigation and let the excess flow into the lake.
A 2023 report put the surface area at 318 square miles (823.6 km2); the lake is about 15 by 35 miles (24 by 56 km) at its widest and longest.
The lake surface is 236.0 ft (71.9 m) below sea level as of January 2018.
In the 1950s and 1960s the area became a resort destination, with more than 1.5 million visitors annually at the peak.
After 1999, the lake began to shrink as local agriculture used the water more efficiently, so less runoff flowed into the lake.
As the lake bed became exposed, winds sent clouds of toxic dust into nearby communities.
In 2019 the water of the Salton Sea had a salinity of about 70 grams per liter, double the salinity of the Pacific Ocean (35 g/L).
